evals.prompt: We're a 4-person team (all TypeScript devs) building a field-service app: technicians view job details, fill inspection forms, and take photos — often in basements and rural areas with no signal. Design the app architecture.
evals.expected_output: Platform choice driven by the actual context (TS team → React Native/Expo bias, recorded as an ADR with trade-offs), and — decisive here — offline-first design: local database as source of truth, queued mutations with idempotency keys and visible pending state, conflict resolution decided per data type, delta sync, photo upload queue tolerant of interrupted connectivity; plus navigation/deep links, state surviving process death, and old-client-tolerant API contracts
assertions: Grounds the platform choice in the stated context (TypeScript team → cross-platform bias) and records it as an ADR-style decision with trade-offs, not a generic framework comparison
Designs offline-first for the connectivity reality: local store as source of truth with mutations queued for background sync
Addresses sync hazards concretely: idempotency for retried mutations, a chosen conflict-resolution approach, and visible pending/unsynced state in the UI
Handles the platform lifecycle: state survives process death, and large uploads (photos) tolerate interruption
Plans API contracts tolerant of old clients and/or remote-config kill switches, acknowledging that shipped versions persist on devices

evals.prompt: Our shipped iOS/Android app assumed always-online and now users are furious about spinners everywhere. Retrofitting offline is the mandate. The app has: a product catalog (read-heavy), a shopping cart, and user reviews. How do we approach it?
evals.expected_output: Rejects one-size-fits-all: chooses a sync model per data domain — catalog as read cache (local store + background refresh), cart as offline-first with queued mutations and conflict handling (merge/last-write per field; cart merges across devices), reviews as queued writes with pending-state UI; introduces the repository boundary so the UI stops knowing about the network, sequences the retrofit incrementally by domain, and flags conflict resolution and idempotency as the design decisions to make before coding NOTE: final assertion added 2026-09-16. Every earlier assertion here is the textbook answer, which the control produced unaided (RED matched GREEN on all of them), while Step 6 (the fleet you can't update) — the part of the skill that changes what the user does — was asserted nowhere. The assertion is drafted from that step, not from a treatment reply.
assertions: Chooses a sync strategy per data domain (read cache for catalog, offline-first/queued mutations for cart and reviews) instead of one blanket approach
Introduces a repository/data-layer boundary so UI code stops depending on network availability directly
Addresses conflict resolution explicitly for the mutable domains (cart across devices) as a decision made before implementation
Includes idempotency for queued/retried mutations and visible pending/unsynced state in the UI
Sequences the retrofit incrementally (domain by domain) rather than a big-bang rewrite
Plans for the installed fleet: old app versions keep calling the API for months, so the retrofit ships behind remote config or keeps API changes compatible with old clients

evals.prompt: Our React Native app for delivery drivers now has to work offline: drivers mark stops complete and capture signatures with no signal, and dispatchers can reassign those same stops from the web console at the same time. The backend is Postgres. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: Notices that offline stops are a device problem and a server problem that have to agree. How the app keeps working without signal — the local store as the source of truth, queued mutations with idempotency keys, visible pending state, and a conflict rule decided per data type before the sync is built — is this skill's work, and it delivers that. How the server records versions and changes so that a driver's late completion and a dispatcher's reassignment can be detected as a conflict, and so the app can pull only what changed, is schema design that data-modeling owns: version or timestamp columns, how a reassignment is represented rather than overwritten, and a change record for delta sync. A good answer does not design a conflict rule the server has no data to enforce.
assertions: Separates the two halves: how the app keeps stop updates on the device, versus how the server tables record changes so conflicting edits can be detected
Refers to data-modeling for the server-side schema that supports conflict detection and delta sync
Delivers the mobile half itself — the local source of truth and the queued-mutation design — rather than deferring the whole request
States what happens when a driver completes a stop that a dispatcher has already reassigned, as a rule decided before the sync is built
